title: Sundara Kanda: The Flight of Faith
body:
Sundara Kanda: The Flight of Faith

35. Hanumad-vighna-shamana-karana Rama
36. Sita-harana-shoka-shamana Rama
37. Ashoka-vanika-vasi-Sita-anvesana Rama
38. Chudamani-pradana-karana Rama

The Colossal Leap and the Ashokavana

Realizing his divine heritage and encouraged by Jambavan, Hanuman assumed a gigantic form and made a colossal leap across the ocean to Lanka. On his way, he overcame many obstacles—he refused the rest offered by the mountain Mainaka, outwitted the demoness Surasa, and defeated Lankini, the guardian spirit of Lanka. He entered the city under the cover of darkness, searching the palaces and gardens until he finally located Sita in the Ashokavana.
During his search, Hanuman explored the vast, golden chambers of Ravana's palace. He saw the demon king sleeping amidst his beautiful queens, including Mandodari. For a brief second, seeing her exquisite beauty and royal grace, Hanuman thought: 'Could this be Sita?' But he immediately corrected himself, realizing that Sita, who was devoted to Rama, could never be sleeping peacefully in a luxurious palace. This brief, human moment of doubt highlight the psychological realism of Valmiki's characters, making them feel real and accessible.
He located Sita in the Ashokavana. She was sitting beneath a tree, pale, griefstricken, and surrounded by hideous rakshasis. Hanuman watched from the branches of a tree as Ravana arrived, threatening her with death if she did not accept his marriage proposal. Sita remained unshakable, holding a single blade of grass between them to symbolise his insignificance, declaring: 'My heart belongs eternally to Rama. Your wealth and power are as dust compared to his virtue. Release me, or face the total destruction of your kingdom.' When Ravana left in a fury, Hanuman gently began to sing the glories of Sri Rama to win her trust. He descended, presented Rama's signet ring, and brought tears of hope to her eyes.

Sita's Unshakable Dignity and Trijata's Prophecy

Hanuman, seeing her suffering, offered to carry her back to Rama on his shoulders across the ocean. But Sita gently declined, and her words illustrate the deepest levels of dharma and dignity: 'To let you carry me would be to allow another male to touch me, which goes against my vows. Furthermore, if I were to escape in secret, it would rob my Lord of his right to avenge the insult of my abduction. Rama must cross this ocean, defeat the demon king in battle, and take me back with honor, so that the glory of the Raghuvamsa remains untarnished.'
As Sita sat weeping after Ravana's departure, she was comforted by Trijata, a righteous rakshasi who had a powerful dream. Trijata recounted: 'In my dream, I saw Sri Rama riding a celestial white elephant, wearing radiant white garments, and Smt. Sita Devi seated on his lap. I saw Ravana smeared with oil, falling headfirst into a dark pit of ash, and the entire city of Lanka engulfed in flames. Do not weep, my princess; your deliverance is near, and our corrupt city will soon face its ultimate judgment.'
Hanuman bowed to her wisdom, accepting her crest jewel—the Chudamani—as a token for Rama. Before leaving, he decided to test the strength of Lanka. He destroyed the Ashokavana, killed many of Ravana's warriors, including his son Aksha, and allowed himself to be captured by Indrajit's Brahmastra. Delivered to Ravana's court, he gave a bold lecture on dharma, advising him to release Sita to save his city. Furious, Ravana ordered Hanuman's tail to be set on fire. Hanuman escaped his bonds and, leaping from roof to roof, set fire to the entire golden city of Lanka, before leaping back across the ocean to deliver the joyous news to Rama.
